subject: Ledgerfern — software for insolvency teams, though not quite a normal SaaS pitch
body:
Hi — I'm Marta, cofounder of Ledgerfern in Hamburg. We build case-management software for insolvency practitioners: creditor claims come in as PDFs, spreadsheets and occasionally photographs of handwritten forms. Our product reconciles those claims, flags duplicates and generates the reporting files courts require. The customer is the insolvency firm, not the debtor or creditor.

The bit that makes us slightly unusual is the onboarding. For a firm's first case, our operations team helps clean the historical records. People sometimes call us a tech-enabled service because of that. But firms subsequently run cases themselves, and 86% of our revenue is annual software subscriptions; the rest is separately priced migration work. We don't take a percentage of recovered assets.

We have 19 paying firms across Germany and the Netherlands, €412k ARR and 117 active cases on the platform. Seven firms have expanded their seat count. No customer has left yet, although our oldest subscription is only 14 months old, so I wouldn't pretend that's a mature retention cohort. Median deployment has fallen from eight weeks to three.

My cofounder, Emil, built document infrastructure at a European accounting-software company. I spent nine years running operations at an insolvency practice. There are seven of us now, including two people who do migrations; we want the next three hires to be engineering rather than more implementation staff.

We're raising a €3m seed round after a €450k angel round in 2024. We are looking for a lead investing €1.5–2m. About €650k is verbally committed by existing angels, not signed. The money gets us through the German court integrations and into two additional European markets. We aren't building a law firm or buying practices.

I realise the services component may put us just outside your usual pattern. Would you take a look at the deck and tell me whether this is worth a conversation? I can send the subscription/migration revenue split and cohort data too. We have no artificial deadline; I'd rather find someone comfortable with an unglamorous workflow than rush this.

subject: Your fund's LP reporting: can we earn the next renewal?
body:
Hello — I'm Priya, founder of Fundrelay. I'm writing about your own fund operations, not to pitch an investment. We provide LP-reporting software to venture managers, and I wondered whether your associate team still spends quarter-end stitching together portfolio spreadsheets.

The product imports administrator files, tracks portfolio updates and produces a branded LP report with an approval trail. We don't replace your administrator. We replace the shared folder called final_final_v3, which I suspect exists at almost every fund.

We now serve 63 fund managers representing 181 vehicles. Our customers produced 740 quarterly reports through Fundrelay last year, and our median implementation took nine business days. I can share two references from managers of a similar size if useful.

Our team is 12 people in Dublin. I previously managed reporting at a fund administrator, and my cofounder built permissions systems for enterprise software. You would work directly with our implementation lead, not a rotating outsourced support team.

For completeness, we closed our €4m seed round last September. That round is finished, we are not raising, and there is no allocation to discuss. I'm mentioning it only because procurement teams often ask whether we have enough runway to support a multi-year contract.

What I'd like is a 25-minute demo with whoever owns LP reporting. Annual plans start at €18,000 per management company. If you can route this to your CFO or operations lead, I'll send a sample report using dummy data; no need to upload anything confidential.

If this isn't a current project, just reply 'later' and I'll leave you alone until your next renewal window. Thanks for reading a longer note than a vendor probably deserves.

subject: Celine at QueryMantle suggested we talk — Dockscript Series A
body:
Hi Alex,

Celine Roux, cofounder of your portfolio company QueryMantle, suggested I email you directly. We've worked together since our infrastructure days at a payments company, and she said she'd already sent you a quick note about Dockscript. She's happy to join a first conversation if useful.

Dockscript is a developer platform for testing database migrations against realistic production workloads before they ship. We create isolated, masked test environments, run the proposed migration and surface locking, latency and compatibility issues inside the pull request. We sell subscriptions to engineering teams; there is no consulting or hardware component.

We're based in Lyon, with all eight employees in France and Germany. Our first paid customer signed 19 months ago. We now have 34 paying companies and €1.46m ARR, up from €510k a year ago. Median implementation time is four days, and 27 customers connected a second database within their first quarter.

Net revenue retention is 132%, gross margin is 88%, and we've had one customer churn, following an acquisition. Those numbers are still from a small base, so I don't want to oversell them. Our largest customer contributes 13% of ARR; three reference customers have agreed to speak with prospective investors.

My cofounder Boris led database reliability at a European logistics platform. I previously built and sold deployment software to mid-market engineering teams. Four of our six engineers have worked on database internals, and our first commercial hire joined in January. Neither of us is doing this as a side project.

We're raising a €6m Series A after a €1.4m seed round two years ago. We're looking for a €2–3m lead, with existing investors planning to contribute €1.2m. The proceeds fund a US sales hire, support for two additional database engines and roughly 24 months of runway. We aren't setting an artificial deadline, but first partner meetings are happening next week.

I've attached the deck and a one-page metrics summary. Would you and the relevant partner have 30 minutes on Tuesday or Thursday? Celine said your team asks good questions about developer adoption versus actual buying intent, which is exactly the conversation I'd like to have.

Thanks,
Leila

subject: FleetLedger — €24m minority growth investment
body:
Dear investment team,

I'm the founder and CEO of FleetLedger, headquartered in Milan. We've spent the last eleven years building the operating software used by regional freight carriers to manage dispatch, invoicing, driver documentation and customer service. I realise this is larger than a typical early-stage round, but wanted to put it on your radar directly.

The product is subscription software, with integrations to customers' existing telematics providers. We do not manufacture devices or operate trucks. Our customers are mostly family-owned carriers with 40–400 vehicles, where replacing the founder's spreadsheet is still a surprisingly good sales pitch.

Today we serve 612 customers across Italy, Spain and France. Last year's revenue was €18.6m, of which 94% was recurring, and adjusted EBITDA was €4.1m. We grew revenue 19% year on year, with 108% net revenue retention. Our largest customer accounts for less than 2% of revenue.

We have 96 employees. My cofounder still leads product, our COO previously managed a national transport software business, and our finance director joined from a listed ERP vendor. The business is founder-controlled and has never raised venture capital; our only external financing is a small bank facility.

We're seeking a €24m minority growth-equity investment. Approximately €16m would fund two acquisitions and our launch in Germany, with €8m providing partial founder liquidity. We're targeting private-equity and growth investors able to take the full position or write a minimum €8m cheque as part of a small syndicate.

An adviser has prepared a financial model, quality-of-earnings materials and a detailed integration plan for both acquisition targets. We are not presenting this as a seed or Series A opportunity. It is a profitable consolidation platform, and the governance package would reflect that.

If this falls within your mandate, could we arrange a conversation with the partner covering software growth investments? I can send the information memorandum following an NDA. If not, a pointer to an appropriate investor would be appreciated.

Best regards,
Matteo

subject: Benchsignal — first round, although everyone calls it something different
body:
Hello — I'm Dario, cofounder of Benchsignal in Rotterdam. I found your fund while looking for investors who understand developer infrastructure rather than another AI wrapper. This is a cold email, and a slightly longer one because our stage needs explaining.

We build a regression-testing service for teams shipping speech models. Customers replay consented audio samples against a new model version, compare failure rates by accent and environment, and block a release if quality drops. We sell the software to engineering teams; we don't provide human labeling or microphones.

The hosted version went live eleven weeks ago. There are 14 teams in the workspace, six running weekly tests and three doing pilots. We have invoiced €9,600 in total for pilot access, but none has signed an annual subscription. Two procurement processes are underway. Calling that ARR would be creative, so I won't.

Usage looks more encouraging: 82,000 test minutes last month, up from 31,000 in the previous month. One pilot has put our check into its release pipeline. Another still downloads our CSV and does the review manually. The numbers include free accounts, which matters.

There are three of us, all based in the Netherlands. I built test infrastructure at a European speech-software company; my cofounder Yara did applied acoustics research, and our third teammate owns the integrations. We have no full-time sales hire and no US entity.

We've bootstrapped with savings and a €60k innovation grant. We're now raising our first outside round of €1.8m, with a hoped-for €1.2m lead cheque. One angel calls it seed; another says we should finish the pilots and raise pre-seed. No institutional investor has committed, and we haven't settled the instrument or valuation.

The money would give us about 20 months to convert pilots, add private-cloud deployment and hire one solutions engineer. I can send the pilot agreements, cohort table and a rough deck. Would you want to look now, or is recurring revenue a prerequisite? Either answer would help us stop guessing.

My cofounder Emil spent eight years building forwarding software, and I previously ran invoice operations for a regional logistics group. We are 13 people, all in Germany or Denmark. Nine are product and engineering; the commercial team is still small enough that I do most late-stage demos.

subject: Flagquarry seed — the incident that happens after rollback
body:
Hi, I'm Bram, cofounder of Flagquarry in Amsterdam. Cold email, sorry. I found your fund while looking for investors who actually distinguish developer tooling from outsourced engineering. We sell software, not engineering hours.

Flagquarry tracks configuration changes across feature flags, environment variables and deployment settings. When a service breaks, teams can see what changed outside the codebase and revert the relevant setting with an approval trail. Most observability products show the symptom; we try to make the cause painfully obvious.

We launched the paid product nine months ago. Today we have 31 paying companies, €420k ARR and 89% gross margin. Six customers have expanded from one team to company-wide use. The median deployment takes a day, although two larger accounts took closer to a month because of security reviews.

Growth hasn't been perfectly tidy. Three small customers churned when their teams were cut, and one account represents 18% of ARR. We are not calling either of those things 'enterprise validation.' New bookings in the last quarter were €118k of annual recurring revenue, mostly inbound from our open-source configuration diff library.

My cofounder Vera built internal release infrastructure at a European payments processor. I led developer experience at a database company. There are five of us, all based in the Netherlands, and nobody is doing consulting on the side to make these numbers work.

We're raising a €3.5m seed, seeking a €1.5–2.5m lead investment. We have 14 months of runway before the raise, so this is not a Friday emergency. The money goes mainly into two integration engineers and a first commercial hire; we want to test repeatable sales before adding a full sales team.

Here's the deck: https://flagquarry.example/seed. It includes the customer cohorts and the concentration breakdown. Would you have 25 minutes next week? Happy to do a live demo rather than narrate 20 slides.

subject: Weekenderly seed — the group chat finally makes a plan
body:
Hi Alex,

I'm Esme, co-founder of Weekenderly in Austin. I realise a consumer company may not be your usual thing, but I wanted to write directly rather than try to squeeze us into a software-for-businesses story. We're building an app that helps friends choose something to do together, agree on a time, and actually turn up. Think fewer abandoned polls and fewer Friday nights spent asking 'so what's the plan?'

The product combines shared availability with a small catalogue of local activities. A group can shortlist options, vote, and book without one friend becoming the unpaid organiser. People can use the basic planning tools free; a $6 monthly subscription adds recurring groups, calendar sync and private itineraries. Our buyers are individuals. Restaurants and venues can appear in discovery, but we do not sell them software or charge them subscriptions.

We launched publicly eight months ago and now have 94,000 registered users, 23,600 monthly active users and 3,100 paying subscribers. Subscription revenue last month was $18,200 after refunds. Of groups that create their first plan, 38% create another within 30 days. That's not where we want retention to end up, but it has improved from 24% in our first cohort. We can share the raw cohort tables, not just the upward-sloping slide.

Growth has come mostly from invites: each active organiser brings an average of 3.8 friends into their first group. We have also spent $42,000 testing paid acquisition across three cities. Those campaigns were uneven, and we've stopped the channels where subscriber payback looked longer than a year. We're focused on Austin and Denver before adding another city, because a thin catalogue makes the app feel empty even when the planning tools work.

There are six of us. I previously ran a consumer subscription product at a travel startup, and my co-founder, Kieran Moss, built calendar infrastructure at a scheduling company. Our first engineer has shipped two social apps; our community lead spent five years running local events. We all work from Austin. Nobody on the team is pretending this is enterprise SaaS with a different landing page.

We're raising a $3.8m seed, with $900k committed by angels, and would like one institutional investor to put in roughly €1.5m. That gives us 20 months to improve retention, launch two additional cities, and test whether the subscription can support a sustainable consumer business. We aren't counting hypothetical venue revenue in the plan. The deck includes our budget and a downside case with no improvement in acquisition costs.

Would you consider a conversation, even if only to tell us where you think the model breaks? I've attached the deck and a three-minute demo. If consumer is a firm no, I understand — a quick pass is genuinely more useful than leaving this in limbo. Thanks for reading a longer note than your inbox probably needed.

subject: Millwarden Series A — software for independent flour mills
body:
Hello Alex,

I'm Sabine, co-founder of Millwarden in Lyon. This is a cold approach after reading about your focus on vertical software. We build the operating system for independent flour mills: purchasing grain, scheduling production, recording quality results, and tracing which lots went into which customer orders. There is no equipment sale hidden in the business; we connect to existing systems and charge a software subscription.

A surprising amount of this workflow still lives in spreadsheets, paper binders and one person's memory. A mill can run a modern production line and still need three people to reconstruct a batch history for an audit. We start with traceability because it has a clear buyer and a painful deadline, then expand into inventory and production planning. We do not need customers to replace their accounting software to get value.

Today we serve 43 paying sites across France, Belgium and the US. ARR is €1.46m, up 91% year over year, with 79% gross margin. Net revenue retention is 116%, and two customers have churned in the last twelve months: one plant closed, and one reverted to its parent's internal system. Our top customer represents 12% of ARR. The US sites account for 18% of revenue and are supported from our existing team.

The less flattering detail is onboarding. Median time to go live is seven weeks, and two implementations last quarter took more than twelve. Historic lot data is usually the bottleneck. We've built import tools that should help, but we're not yet claiming the problem is solved. Implementation fees are separate from ARR and represented €112k of revenue last year; we don't pad subscription numbers with those fees.

We're a team of twelve. I spent eight years managing software delivery for food processors, while my co-founder, Benicio Ward, led engineering at an industrial workflow software company. Our head of customer success previously ran quality assurance at a milling group. Product and engineering are in Lyon, and we use specialist contractors for a few integrations rather than carrying a large services bench.

We're raising a €6m Series A to build a repeatable US sales motion and reduce implementation effort. We are seeking a lead investing €2.5–3.5m, with existing seed investors planning to participate for €1m. We have about fourteen months of runway, so this is not a rescue round or a Friday deadline. We'd rather find someone who understands the economics of a narrow vertical than add ten adjacent markets to make the TAM slide bigger.

I've attached the deck, monthly revenue bridge and a sample implementation plan. Would you be open to a 30-minute call in the next couple of weeks? If useful, we can arrange references with one new customer and one that's been with us for two years. Thank you, Sabine.
